entries.507d55ea7224439dc48a4b312184b5e0abbf27e1: <div sID="gen19962" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Hos.14" sID="Hos.14"/> <div eID="gen19962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19963" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19964" type="x-p"/> The strain of this chapter differs from that of the foregoing chapters. Those were generally made up of reproofs for sin and threatenings of wrath; but this is made up of exhortations to repentance and promises of mercy, and with these the prophet closes; for all the foregoing convictions and terrors he had spoken were designed to prepare and make way for these. He wounds that he may heal. The Spirit convinces that he may comfort. This chapter is a lesson for penitents; and some such there were in Israel at this day, bad as things were. We have here, I. Directions in repenting, what to do and what to say, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.1-Hos.14.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. Encouragements to repent taken from God's readiness to receive returning sinners (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.4">ver. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.8">8</reference>) and the comforts he has treasured up for them, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.5-Hos.14.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. III. A solemn recommendation of these things to our serious thoughts, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.9">ver. 9</reference>.
entries.aea140a1c86354e67a200c1a75cfa12edd1309c2: <div eID="gen19964" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19963" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Penitents Encouraged. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen19965" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> O Israel, return unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God; for thou hast fallen by thine iniquity. <hi type="super">2</hi> Take with you words, and turn to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : say unto him, Take away all iniquity, and receive <hi type="italic">us</hi> graciously: so will we render the calves of our lips. <hi type="super">3</hi> Asshur shall not save us; we will not ride upon horses: neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, <hi type="italic">Ye are</hi> our gods: for in thee the fatherless findeth mercy. <div eID="gen19965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19966" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen19966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19967" type="x-p"/> I. A kind invitation given to sinners to repent, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.1">v. 1</reference>. It is directed to Israel, God's professing people. They are called to <hi type="italic">return.</hi> Note, Conversion must be preached even to those that are within the pale of the church as well as to heathen. "Thou are Israel, and therefore art bound to thy God in duty, gratitude, and interest; thy revolt from him is so much the more heinous, and thy return to him so much the more necessary." Let Israel see, 1. What work he has made for repentance: "<hi type="italic">Thou has fallen by thy iniquity." Thou has stumbled;</hi> so some read it. Their idols were their <hi type="italic">stumbling-blocks.</hi> "Thou has fallen from God into sin, fallen off from all good, fallen down under the load of guilt and the curse." Note, Sin is a fall; and it concerns those that have fallen by sin to get up again by repentance. 2. What work he has to do in his repentance: "<hi type="italic">Return to the Lord thy God;</hi> return to him as <hi type="italic">the Lord</hi> whom thou has a dependence upon, as <hi type="italic">thy God,</hi> thine in covenant, whom thou has an interest in." Note, It is the great concern of those that have revolted from God to <hi type="italic">return to God,</hi> and so to do their <hi type="italic">first works.</hi> "Return to him from whom thou has fallen, and who alone is able to raise thee up. Return <hi type="italic">even to the Lord,</hi> or <hi type="italic">quite home</hi> to the Lord; do not only look to him, or take some steps towards him, but make thorough work of it." The ancient Jews had a saying grounded on this, <hi type="italic">Repentance is a great thing, for it brings men quite up to the throne of glory.</hi> <div eID="gen19967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19968" type="x-p"/> II. Necessary instructions given them how to repent. 1. They must bethink themselves what to say to God when they come to him: <hi type="italic">Take with you words.</hi> They are required to bring, not sacrifices and offerings, but penitential prayers and supplications, the <hi type="italic">fruit of thy lips,</hi> yet not of the lips only, but of the heart, else words are but wind. One of the rabbin says, They must be such words as proceed <hi type="italic">from what is spoken first in the inner man;</hi> the heart must dictate to the tongue. We must take good words with us, by taking good thoughts and good affections with us. <hi type="italic">Verbaque prævisam rem non invita sequentur—Those who master a subject are seldom at a loss for language.</hi> Note, When we come to God we should consider what we have to say to him; for, if we come without an errand, we are likely to go without an answer. <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.10">Ezra ix. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">What shall we say?</hi> We must take with us words from the scripture, take them from the Spirit of grace and supplication, who teaches us to cry, Abba, Father, and makes intercession in us. 2. They must bethink themselves what to do. They must not only take with them words, but must <hi type="italic">turn to the Lord;</hi> inwardly in their hearts, outwardly in their lives. <div eID="gen19968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19969" type="x-p"/> III. For their assistance herein, and encouragement, God is pleased to put words into their mouths, to teach them what they shall say. Surely we may hope to speed with God, when he himself has ordered our address to be drawn up ready to our hands, and his own Spirit has indited it for us; and no doubt we shall speed if the workings of our souls agree with the words here recommended to us. They are, <div eID="gen19969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19970" type="x-p"/> 1. Petitioning words. Two things we are here directed to petition for:—(1.) To be acquitted from guilt. When we return to the Lord we must say to him, Lord, <hi type="italic">take away all iniquity.</hi> They were now smarting for sin, under the load of affliction, but are taught to pray, not as Pharaoh, Take away <hi type="italic">this death,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">Take away this</hi> sin. Note, When we are in affliction we should be more concerned for the forgiveness of our sins than for the removal of our trouble. "<hi type="italic">Take away iniquity,</hi> lift it off as a <hi type="italic">burden</hi> we are ready to sink under or as the stumbling-block which we have often fallen over. Lord, take it away, that it may not appear against us, to our confusion and condemnation. Take it all away by a free and full remission, for we cannot pretend to strike any of it off by a satisfaction of our own." When God pardons sin he pardons <hi type="italic">all,</hi> that <hi type="italic">great debt;</hi> and when we pray against sin we must pray against it all and not except any. (2.) To be accepted as righteous in God's sight: "<hi type="italic">Receive us graciously.</hi> Let us have thy favour and love, and have thou respect to us and to our performances. Receive our prayer graciously; be well pleased with that good which by thy grace we are enabled to do." <hi type="italic">Take good</hi> (so the word is); take it to bestow upon us, so the margin reads it—<hi type="italic">Give good.</hi> This follows upon the petition for the taking away of iniquity; for, till iniquity is taken away, we have no reason to expect any good from God, but the taking away of iniquity makes way for the conferring of good <hi type="italic">removendo prohibens—by taking that out of the way which hindered. Give good;</hi> they do not say what good, but refer themselves to God; it is not good of the world's showing (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Ps. iv. 6</reference>), but good of God's giving. "<hi type="italic">Give good,</hi> that good which we have forfeited, and which thou has promised, and which the necessity of our case calls for." Note, God's gracious acceptance, and the blessed fruits and tokens of that acceptance, are to be earnestly desired and prayed for by us in our returning to God. "<hi type="italic">Give good,</hi> that good which will make us good and keep us from returning to iniquity again." <div eID="gen19970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19971" type="x-p"/> 2. Promising words. These also are put into their mouths, not to move God, or to oblige him to show them mercy, but to move themselves, and oblige themselves to returns of duty. Note, Our prayers for pardon and acceptance with God should be always accompanied with sincere purposes and vows of new obedience. Two things they are to promise and vow:—(1.) Thanksgiving. "Pardon our sins, and accept of us, so <hi type="italic">will we render the calves of our lips.</hi>" The <hi type="italic">fruit of our lips</hi> (so the LXX.), a word they used for <hi type="italic">burnt-offerings,</hi> and so it agrees with the Hebrew. The apostle quotes this phrase (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb. xiii. 15</reference>), and by the <hi type="italic">fruit of our lips</hi> understands the <hi type="italic">sacrifice of praise to God, giving thanks to his name.</hi> Note, Praise and thanksgiving are our spiritual sacrifice, and, if they come from an upright heart, shall please the Lord <hi type="italic">better than an ox or bullock,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.69.30">Ps. lxxix. 30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.32">32</reference>. And the sense of our pardon and acceptance with God will enlarge our hearts in praise and thankfulness. Those that are <hi type="italic">received graciously</hi> may, and must, <hi type="italic">render the calves of their lips</hi>—poor returns for rich receivings, yet, if sincere, more acceptable than the calves of the stall. (2.) Amendment of life. They are taught to promise, not only verbal acknowledgements, but a real reformation. And we are taught here, [1.] In our returns to God to covenant against sin. We cannot expect that God should take it away by forgiving it if we do not put it away by forsaking it. [2.] To be particular in our covenants and resolutions against sin, as we ought to be in our confession, because deceit lies in generals. [3.] To covenant especially and expressly against those sins which we have been most subject to, which have most easily beset us, and which we have been most frequently overcome by. We must keep ourselves from, and therefore must thus fortify ourselves against, <hi type="italic">our own iniquity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.18.23">Ps. xviii. 23</reference>. The sin they here covenant against, owning thereby that they had been guilty of it, is giving that glory to another which is due to God only; this they promise they will never do, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> By putting that confidence in creatures which should be put in God only. They will not trust to their alliances abroad: <hi type="italic">Asshur</hi> (that is, Assyria) <hi type="italic">shall not save us.</hi> "We will not court the help of the Assyrians when we are in distress, as we have done (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.13">ch. v. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.7.11">vii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.9">viii. 9</reference>); we will not contract for it, nor will we confide in it, or depend upon it. Having a God to go to, a God all-sufficient to trust to, we scorn to be beholden to the Assyrians for help." They will not trust to their warlike preparations at home, especially not those which they were forbidden to multiply: "<hi type="italic">We will not ride upon horses,</hi> that is, we will not make court to Egypt," for thence they fetched their horses, <reference osisRef="Deut.17.16 Isa.30.16">Deut. xvii. 16; Isa. xxx. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1-Isa.31.3">xxxi. 1, 3</reference>. "When our enemies invade us we will depend upon our God to succour our infantry, and will be in no care to remount our cavalry." Or, "We will not <hi type="italic">post on horseback,</hi> for haste, from one creature to another, to seek relief, but will take the nearest way, and the only sure way, by addressing ourselves to God," <reference osisRef="Isa.20.5">Isa. xx. 5</reference>. Note, True repentance takes us off from trusting to an arm of flesh, and brings us to rely on God only for all the good we stand in need of. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Nor will they do it by paying that homage to creatures which is due to God only. We <hi type="italic">will not say any more to the works of our hands, You are our gods.</hi> They must promise never to worship idols again, and for a good reason, because it is the most absurd and senseless thing in the world to pray to that as a god which is the work of our hands. We must promise that we will not set our hearts upon the gains of this world, nor pride ourselves in our external performances in religion, for that is, in effect, to say to the work of our hands, <hi type="italic">You are our gods.</hi> <div eID="gen19971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19972" type="x-p"/> 3. Pleading words are here put into their mouths: For <hi type="italic">in thee the fatherless find mercy.</hi> We must take our encouragement in prayer, not from any merit God finds in us, but purely from the mercy we hope to find in God. This contains in itself a great truth, that God takes special care of fatherless children, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.4-Ps.68.5">Ps. lxviii. 4, 5</reference>. So he did in his law, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.22">Exod. xxii. 22</reference>. So he does in his providence, <reference osisRef="Ps.27.10">Ps. xxvii. 10</reference>. It is God's prerogative to help the helpless. In him there is mercy for such, for they are proper objects of mercy. In him they find it; there it is laid up for them, and there they must seek it; <hi type="italic">seek and you shall find.</hi> It comes in here as a good plea for mercy and grace and an encouraging one to their faith. (1.) They plead the distress of their state and condition: "We are fatherless orphans, destitute of help." Those may expect to find help in God that are truly sensible of their helplessness in themselves and are willing to acknowledge it. This is a good step towards comfort. "If we have not yet boldness to call God <hi type="italic">Father,</hi> yet we look upon ourselves as fatherless without him, and therefore lay ourselves at his feet, to be looked upon by him with compassion." (2.) They plead God's wonted lovingkindness to such as were in that condition: <hi type="italic">With thee the fatherless</hi> not only may find, but <hi type="italic">does find,</hi> and shall find, <hi type="italic">mercy.</hi> It is a great encouragement to our faith and hope, in returning to God, that it is his glory to father the fatherless and help the helpless.
entries.6225e402bebb9d4127555bb088832fcda4c4e83d: <div eID="gen19972" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Assurance of Mercy; Repentance of Ephraim. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen19973" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely: for mine anger is turned away from him. <hi type="super">5</hi> I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon. <hi type="super">6</hi> His branches shall spread, and his beauty shall be as the olive tree, and his smell as Lebanon. <hi type="super">7</hi> They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive <hi type="italic">as</hi> the corn, and grow as the vine: the scent thereof <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> as the wine of Lebanon. <div eID="gen19973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19974" type="x-p"/> We have here an answer of peace to the prayers of returning Israel. They seek God's face, and they shall not <hi type="italic">seek in vain.</hi> God will be sure to meet those in a way of mercy who return to him in a way of duty. If we speak to God in good prayers, God will speak to us in good promises, as he <hi type="italic">answered the angel with good words and comfortable words,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.1.13">Zech. i. 13</reference>. If we take with us the foregoing words in our coming to God, we may take home with us these following words for our faith to feast upon; and see how these answer those. <div eID="gen19974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19975" type="x-p"/> I. Do they dread and deprecate God's displeasure, and therefore return to him? He assures them that, upon their submission, his <hi type="italic">anger is turned away from them.</hi> This is laid as the ground of all the other favours here promised. I will do so and so, for my <hi type="italic">anger is turned away,</hi> and thereby a door is opened for all good to flow to them, <reference osisRef="Isa.12.1">Isa. xii. 1</reference>. Note, Though God is justly and greatly angry with sinners, yet he is not implacable in his anger; it may be turned away; it shall be turned away, from those that turn away from their iniquity. God will be reconciled to those that are reconciled to him and to his whole will. <div eID="gen19975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19976" type="x-p"/> II. Do they pray for the <hi type="italic">taking away of iniquity?</hi> He assures them that he will <hi type="italic">heal their backslidings;</hi> so he promised, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.22">Jer. iii. 22</reference>. Note, Though backslidings from God are the dangerous diseases and wounds of the soul, yet they are not incurable, for God has graciously promised that if backsliding sinners will apply to him as their physician, and comply with his methods, he will heal their backslidings. He will heal the guilt of their backslidings by pardoning mercy and their <hi type="italic">bent to backslide</hi> by renewing grace. Their <hi type="italic">iniquity</hi> shall <hi type="italic">not be their ruin.</hi> <div eID="gen19976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19977" type="x-p"/> III. Do they pray that God will receive them graciously? In answer to that, behold, it is promised, <hi type="italic">I will love them freely.</hi> God had hated them while they went on sin (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.15">ch. ix. 15</reference>); but now that they return and repent he loves them, not only ceases to be <hi type="italic">angry</hi> with them, but takes complacency in them and designs their good. He <hi type="italic">loves them freely,</hi> with an <hi type="italic">absolute entire</hi> love (so some), so that there are no remains of his former displeasure, with a <hi type="italic">liberal bountiful</hi> love (so others); he will be open-handed in his love to them, and will think nothing too much to bestow upon them or to do for them. Or with a <hi type="italic">cheerful willing</hi> love; he will love them without reluctancy or renitency. He will not say in the day of thy repentance, <hi type="italic">How shall I receive thee again?</hi> as he said in the day of thy apostasy, <hi type="italic">How shall I give thee up?</hi> Or with an <hi type="italic">unmerited preventing</hi> love. Whom God loves he loves <hi type="italic">freely,</hi> not because they deserve it, but of his own good pleasure. He loves because he <hi type="italic">will</hi> love, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.7-Deut.7.8">Deut. vii. 7, 8</reference>. <div eID="gen19977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19978" type="x-p"/> IV. Do they pray that God will <hi type="italic">give good,</hi> will make them good? In answer to that, behold, it is promised, <hi type="italic">I will be as the dew unto Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.14.5">v. 5</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen19978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19979" type="x-p"/> 1. What shall be the favour God will bestow upon them. It is the blessing of their father Jacob, <hi type="italic">God give thee the dew of heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.27.28">Gen. xxvii. 28</reference>. Nay, what they need God will not only give them, but he will himself be <hi type="italic">that</hi> to them, all that which they need: I <hi type="italic">will be as the dew unto Israel.</hi> This ensures <hi type="italic">spiritual blessings in heavenly things;</hi> and it follows upon the healing of their backslidings, for pardoning mercy is always accompanied with renewing grace. Note, To Israelites indeed God himself will be <hi type="italic">as the dew.</hi> He will instruct them; his doctrine shall drop upon them as the dew, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.2">Deut. xxxii. 2</reference>. They shall know more and more of him, for he will come to them <hi type="italic">as the rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Hos. vi. 3</reference>. He will refresh them with his comforts, so that their souls shall be as a <hi type="italic">watered garden,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.11">Isa. lviii. 11</reference>. He will be to true penitents <hi type="italic">as the dew to Israel</hi> when they were in the wilderness, dew that had manna in it, <reference osisRef="Exod.16.14">Exod. xvi. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.11.9">Num. xi. 9</reference>. The graces of the Spirit are the hidden manna, hidden in the dew; God will give them bread from heaven, as he did to Israel in the dew in abundance, <reference osisRef="John.1.16">John i. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen19979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19980" type="x-p"/> 2. What shall be the fruit of that favour which shall be produced in them. The grace thus freely bestowed on them <hi type="italic">shall not be in vain.</hi> Those souls, those Israelites, to whom God is as the dew, on whom his grace distils, <div eID="gen19980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19981" type="x-p"/> (1.) Shall be growing. The bad being by the grace of God made good, they shall by the same grace be made better; for grace, wherever it is true, is growing. [1.] They shall grow upwards, and be more flourishing, <hi type="italic">shall grow as the lily,</hi> or (as some read it) shall <hi type="italic">blossom as the rose.</hi> The growth of the lily, as that of all bulbous roots, is very quick and speedy. The root of the lily seems lost in the ground all winter, but, when it is refreshed with the dews of the spring, it starts up in a little time; so the grace of God improves young converts sometimes very fast. The lily, when it has come to its height, is a lovely flower (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.29">Matt. vi. 29</reference>), so grace is the comeliness of the soul, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.14">Ezek. xvi. 14</reference>. It is the <hi type="italic">beauty of holiness</hi> that is produced by the <hi type="italic">dew of the morning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. [2.] They shall grow downwards, and be more firm. The lily indeed grows fast, and grows fine, but it soon fades and is easily plucked up; and therefore it is here promised to Israel that with the flower of the lily he shall have the root of the cedar: He shall <hi type="italic">cast forth his roots as Lebanon,</hi> as the <hi type="italic">trees of Lebanon,</hi> which, having taken deep root, cannot be plucked up, <reference osisRef="Amos.9.15">Amos ix. 15</reference>. Note, Spiritual growth consists most in the growth of the root, which is out of sight. The more we depend upon Christ and draw sap and virtue from him, the more we act in religion from a principle and the more steadfast and resolved we are in it, the more we <hi type="italic">cast forth our roots.</hi> [3.] They shall grow round about (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">His branches shall spread</hi> on all sides. And (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.7">v. 7</reference>) he shall <hi type="italic">grow as the vine,</hi> whose branches extend furthest of any tree. Joseph was to be <hi type="italic">a fruitful bough,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.49.22">Gen. xlix. 22</reference>. When many are added to the church from without, when a hopeful generation rises up, then Israel's branches spread. When particular believers abound in good works, and increase in the knowledge of God and in every good gift, then their branches may be said to spread. The <hi type="italic">inward man is renewed day by day.</hi> <div eID="gen19981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19982" type="x-p"/> (2.) They shall be graceful and acceptable both to God and man. Grace is the amiable thing, and makes those that have it truly amiable. They are here compared to such trees as are pleasant, [1.] To the sight: <hi type="italic">His beauty shall be as the olive-tree,</hi> which is always green. <hi type="italic">The Lord called thy name a green olive-tree,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.11.16">Jer. xi. 16</reference>. Ordinances are the beauty of the church, and in them it is, and shall be, ever green. Holiness is the beauty of a soul; when those that believe with the heart make profession with the mouth, and justify and adorn that profession with an agreeable conversation, then their beauty is as the olive-tree, <reference osisRef="Ps.52.8">Ps. lii. 8</reference>. It is a promise to the trees of righteousness that their leaf shall not wither. [2.] To the smell: <hi type="italic">His smell</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">as Lebanon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.6">v. 6</reference>) and his <hi type="italic">scent as the wine of Lebanon,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.14.7">v. 7</reference>. This was the praise of their father Jacob, <hi type="italic">The smell of my son is as the smell of a field which the Lord has blessed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.27.27">Gen. xxvii. 27</reference>. The church is compared to a <hi type="italic">garden of spices</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.4.12">Cant. iv. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.4.14">14</reference>), which <hi type="italic">all her garments smell of.</hi> True believers are <hi type="italic">acceptable to God</hi> and <hi type="italic">approved of men.</hi> God <hi type="italic">smells a sweet savour</hi> from their <hi type="italic">spiritual sacrifices</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.21">Gen. viii. 21</reference>), and they are <hi type="italic">accepted of the multitude of the brethren.</hi> Grace is the perfume of the soul, the perfume of the name, makes it like a precious ointment, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.1">Eccl. vii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">The memorial thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon</hi> (so the margin reads it), not only their reviving comforts now, but their surviving honours when they are gone, shall be as <hi type="italic">the wine of Lebanon,</hi> that has a delicate flavour. Flourishing churches have <hi type="italic">their faith spoken of throughout the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.8">Rom. i. 8</reference>) and <hi type="italic">leave their name to be remembered</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.17">Ps. xlv. 17</reference>); and <hi type="italic">the memory of</hi> flourishing saints is <hi type="italic">blessed,</hi> and shall be so, as theirs who <hi type="italic">by faith obtained a good report.</hi> <div eID="gen19982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19983" type="x-p"/> (3.) They shall be fruitful and useful. The church is compared here to the vine and the olive, which brings forth useful fruits, to the honour of God and man. Nay, the very shadow of the church shall be agreeable (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Those that dwell under his shadow shall return</hi>—under God's <hi type="italic">shadow</hi> (so some), under the shadow of the Messias, so the Chaldee. Believers <hi type="italic">dwell under God's shadow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">Ps. xci. 1</reference>), and there they are and may be safe and easy. But it is rather <hi type="italic">under the shadow of Israel,</hi> under the shadow of the church. Note, God's promises pertain to those, and those only, that dwell under the church's shadow, that attend on God's ordinances and adhere to his people, not those that flee to that shadow only for shelter in a hot gleam, but those that <hi type="italic">dwell under it.</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Ps. xxvii. 4</reference>. We may apply it to particular believers; when a man is effectually brought home to God all that <hi type="italic">dwell under his shadow</hi>—children, servants, subjects, friends. <hi type="italic">This day has salvation come to this house.</hi> Those that dwell under the shadow of the church shall return; their drooping spirits shall return, and they shall be refreshed and comforted. He <hi type="italic">restores my soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.23.3">Ps. xxiii. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">They shall revive as the corn,</hi> which, when it is sown, dies first, and then revives, and <hi type="italic">brings forth much fruit,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.24">John xii. 24</reference>. It is promised that God's people shall be blessings to the world, as corn and wine are. And a very great and valuable mercy it is to be serviceable to our generation. Comfort and honour attend it.
entries.c27447f952e0b332f3dba77d5a31c3ed9b9d9bb3: <div eID="gen19983" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Assurances of Mercy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen19984" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Ephraim <hi type="italic">shall say,</hi> What have I to do any more with idols? I have heard <hi type="italic">him,</hi> and observed him: I <hi type="italic">am</hi> like a green fir tree. From me is thy fruit found. <hi type="super">9</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise, and he shall understand these <hi type="italic">things?</hi> prudent, and he shall know them? for the ways of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">are</hi> right, and the just shall walk in them: but the transgressors shall fall therein. <div eID="gen19984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19985" type="x-p"/> Let us now hear the conclusion of the whole matter. <div eID="gen19985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19986" type="x-p"/> I. Concerning Ephraim; he is spoken of and spoken to, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.8">v. 8</reference>. Here we have, <div eID="gen19986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19987" type="x-p"/> 1. His repentance and reformation: <hi type="italic">Ephraim shall say, What have I to do any more with idols?</hi> As some read it, God here reasons and argues with him, why he should renounce idolatry: "<hi type="italic">O Ephraim! what to me and idols? What concord</hi> or agreement can there be <hi type="italic">between me and idols? What communion between light and darkness, between Christ and Belial?</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.14-2Cor.6.15">2 Cor. vi. 14, 15</reference>. Therefore thou must break off thy league with them if thou wilt come into covenant with me." As we read it, God promises to bring Ephraim and keep him to this: <hi type="italic">Ephraim shall say,</hi> God will put it into his heart to say it, <hi type="italic">What have I to do any more with idols?</hi> He has promised (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.3">v. 3</reference>) not to <hi type="italic">say any more to the works of his hands, You are my gods.</hi> But God's promises to us are much more our security and our strength for the mortifying of sin than our promises to God; and therefore God himself is here <hi type="italic">surety for his servant to good,</hi> will put in into his heart and into his mouth. And, whatever good we say or do at any time, it is he that works it in us. Ephraim had solemnly engaged not to call his idols <hi type="italic">his gods;</hi> but God here engages further for him that he shall resolve to have <hi type="italic">no more to do with them.</hi> He shall abolish them, he shall abandon them, and that with the utmost detestation; for it is necessary not only that in our lives we be turned from sin, but that in our hearts we be turned against sin. See here, (1.) The power of divine grace. Ephraim had been <hi type="italic">joined to his idols</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.4.17">ch. iv. 17</reference>), was so fond of them that one would have thought he could never fall out with them; and yet God will work such a change in him that he shall loathe them as much as ever he loved them. (2.) See the benefit of sanctified afflictions. Ephraim had smarted for his idolatry; it had brought one judgment after another upon him, and this at length is the fruit, even the <hi type="italic">taking away of his sin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.27.9">Isa. xxvii. 9</reference>. (3.) See the nature of repentance; it is a firm and fixed resolution to have no more to do with sin. This is the language of the penitent: "I am ashamed that ever I had to do with sin; but I have had enough of it; I hate it, and by the grace of God I will never have any thing to do with it again, no, not with the occasions of it." Thou shalt say to thy idol, <hi type="italic">Get thee hence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">Isa. xxx. 22</reference>), shalt say to the tempter, <hi type="italic">Get thee behind me, Satan.</hi> <div eID="gen19987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19988" type="x-p"/> 2. The gracious notice God is pleased to take of it: <hi type="italic">I have heard him, and observed him. I have heard, and will look upon him;</hi> so some read it. Note, The God of heaven takes cognizance of the penitent reflections and resolutions of returning sinners. He expects and desires the repentance of sinners, because he has no pleasure in their ruin. <hi type="italic">He looks upon men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.33.27">Job xxxiii. 27</reference>), <hi type="italic">hearkens and hears,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">Jer. viii. 6</reference>. And, if there be any disposition to repent, he is well pleased with it. When <hi type="italic">Ephraim bemoans himself</hi> before God, he is a <hi type="italic">dear son,</hi> he is a <hi type="italic">pleasant child,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jer. xxxi. 20</reference>. He meets penitents with mercy, as the father of the prodigal met his returning son. God <hi type="italic">observed</hi> Ephraim, to see whether he would bring forth fruits meet for this profession of repentance that he made, and whether he would continue in this good mind. He observed him to do him good, and comfort him, according to the exigencies of his case. <div eID="gen19988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19989" type="x-p"/> 3. The mercy of God designed for him, in order to his comfort and perseverance in his resolutions; still God will be all in all to him. Before, Israel was compared to a tree, now God compares himself to one. He will be to his people, (1.) As the branches of a tree: "<hi type="italic">I am like a green fir-tree,</hi> and will be so to thee." The fir-trees, in those countries, were exceedingly large and thick, and a shelter against sun and rain. God will be to all true converts both a delight and a defence; under his protection and influence they shall both dwell in safety and dwell in ease. He with be either <hi type="italic">a sun and a shield</hi> or a <hi type="italic">shade and a shield,</hi> according as their case requires. They shall sit down <hi type="italic">under his shadow with delight,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.2.3">Cant. ii. 3</reference>. He will be so all weathers, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Isa. iv. 6</reference>. (2.) As the root of a tree: <hi type="italic">From me is thy fruit found,</hi> which may be understood either of the fruit brought forth to us (to him we owe all our comforts) or of the fruit brought forth by us—from him we receive grace and strength to enable us to do our duty. Whatever fruits of righteousness we brought forth, all the praise of them is due to God; for he works in us both to will and to do that which is good. <div eID="gen19989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19990" type="x-p"/> II. Concerning every one that hears and reads the words of the prophecy of this book (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who is wise? and he shall understand these things.</hi> Perhaps the prophet was wont to conclude that sermons he preached with these words, and now he closes with them the whole book, in which he has committed to writing some fragments of the many sermons he had preached. Observe, 1. The character of those that do profit by the truths he delivered: <hi type="italic">Who is wise</hi> and <hi type="italic">prudent? He shall understand these things, he shall know them.</hi> Those that set themselves to understand and know these things thereby make it to appear that they are truly wise and prudent, and will thereby be made more so; and, if any do not understand and know them, it is because they are foolish and unwise. Those that are wise in the doing of their duty, that are prudent in practical religion, are most likely to know and understand both the truths and providences of God, which are a mystery to others, <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">The secret of the Lord is with those that fear him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Ps. xxv. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Who is wise?</hi> This intimates a desire that those who read and hear these things would understand them (<hi type="italic">O that they were wise!</hi>) and a complaint that few were so—<hi type="italic">Who has believed our report?</hi> 2. The excellency of these things concerning which we are here instructed: <hi type="italic">The ways of the Lord are right;</hi> and therefore it is our wisdom and duty to know and understand them. The way of God's precepts, in which he requires us to walk, is right, agreeing with the rules of eternal reason and equity and having a direct tendency to our eternal felicity. The ways of God's providence, in which he walks toward us, are all right; no fault is to be found with any thing that God does, for it is all well done. His judgments upon the impenitent, his favours to the penitent, are all right; however they may be perverted and misinterpreted, God will at last be justified and glorified in them all. His <hi type="italic">ways are equal.</hi> 3. The different use which men make of them. (1.) The right ways of God to those that are good are, and will be, a savour of life unto life: <hi type="italic">The just shall walk in them;</hi> they shall conform to the will of God both in his precepts and in his providences, and shall have the comfort of so doing. They shall well understand the mind of God both in his word and in his works; they shall be well reconciled to both, and shall accommodate themselves to God's intention in both. <hi type="italic">The just shall walk</hi> in <hi type="italic">those ways</hi> towards their great end, and shall not come short of it. (2.) The right ways of God will be to those that are wicked a savour of death unto death: <hi type="italic">The transgressors shall fall</hi> not only in their own wrong ways, but even <hi type="italic">in the right ways of the Lord.</hi> Christ, who is a foundation stone to some, is to others a <hi type="italic">stone of stumbling</hi> and a <hi type="italic">rock of offence.</hi> That which was <hi type="italic">ordained to life</hi> becomes through their abuse of it, death to them. God's providences, being not duly improved by them, harden them in sin and contribute to their ruin. God's discovery of himself both in the judgments of his mouth and in the judgments of his hand is to us according as we are affected under it. <hi type="italic">Recipitur ad modum recipientis—What is received influences according to the qualities of the receiver.</hi> The same sun softens wax and hardens clay. But of all transgressors those certainly have the most dangerous fatal falls that fall <hi type="italic">in the ways of God,</hi> that split on the rock of ages, and suck poison out of the balm of Gilead. <hi type="italic">Let the sinners in Zion be afraid</hi> of this.  <chapter eID="Hos.14"/> <div eID="gen19990" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen19650" osisID="Hos" type="book"/>

entries.3b7d0584d973c5e66d806f1732b646699b99c101: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12426"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hos.14.1-Hos.14.9">Ho 14:1-9</reference>. God's Promise of Blessing, on Their Repentance: Their Abandonment of Idolatry Foretold: The Conclusion of the Whole, the Just Shall Walk in God's Ways, but the Transgressor Shall Fall Therein.</title> <div sID="gen22796" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12426"/><hi type="bold">1. fallen by thine iniquity--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.5.5">Ho 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.9">13:9</reference>). <div eID="gen22796" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7f59ddbf84efe22d0a323c3219aab125f82b081: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12427"/><div sID="gen22797" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12427"/><hi type="bold">2. Take with you words--</hi>instead of sacrifices, namely, the words of penitence here put in your mouths by God. "Words," in Hebrew, mean "realities," there being the same term for "words" and "things"; so God implies, He will not accept empty professions (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.36">Psa 78:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.29.13">Is 29:13</reference>). He does not ask costly sacrifices, but words of heartfelt penitence.<div eID="gen22797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22798" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">receive us graciously--</hi>literally "(for) good."<div eID="gen22798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22799" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">calves of our lips--</hi>that is, instead of sacrifices of calves, which we cannot offer to Thee in exile, we present the praises of our lips. Thus the exile, wherein the temple service ceased, prepared the way for the gospel time when the types of the animal sacrifices of the Old Testament being realized in Christ's perfect sacrifice once for all, "the sacrifice of praise to God continually that is the fruit of our lips" (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.14">He 13:14</reference>) takes their place in the New Testament. <div eID="gen22799" type="x-p"/>
entries.18e01f1c59d6fe13fe89bee3b26b551040f9f1ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12428"/><div sID="gen22800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12428"/>3. Three besetting sins of Israel are here renounced, trust in Assyria, application to Egypt for its cavalry (forbidden, <reference osisRef="Deut.17.16">De 17:16</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Hos.7.11">Ho 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.5">11:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Ki 17:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.33.17">Psa 33:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.2">Is 30:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">31:1</reference>), and idolatry.<div eID="gen22800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fatherless--</hi>descriptive of the destitute state of Israel, when severed from God, their true Father. We shall henceforth trust in none but Thee, the only Father of the fatherless, and Helper of the destitute (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">Psa 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.5">68:5</reference>); our nation has experienced Thee such in our helpless state in Egypt, and now in a like state again our only hope is Thy goodness. <div eID="gen22801" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e7e3f9077f9409584db32d635f35536058a380f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12429"/><div sID="gen22802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12429"/>4. God's gracious reply to their self-condemning prayer.<div eID="gen22802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">backsliding--</hi>apostasy: not merely occasional backslidings. God can heal the most desperate sinfulness [Calvin].<div eID="gen22803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">freely--</hi>with a gratuitous, unmerited, and abundant love (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.60-Ezek.16.63">Eze 16:60-63</reference>). So as to the spiritual Israel (<reference osisRef="John.15.16">Joh 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">Ro 3:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.8">5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.10">1Jo 4:10</reference>). <div eID="gen22804" type="x-p"/>
entries.8001504d2b813fe31b6a9719d6d06a19177f7686: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12430"/><div sID="gen22805" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12430"/><hi type="bold">5. as the dew--</hi>which falls copiously in the East, taking the place of the more frequent rains in other regions. God will not be "as the early dew that goeth away," but constant (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.3">Ho 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.6.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.19">Job 29:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.19.12">Pr 19:12</reference>).<div eID="gen22805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22806" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the lily--</hi>No plant is more productive than the lily, one root often producing fifty bulbs [Pliny, Natural History, 21.5]. The common lily is white, consisting of six leaves opening like bells. The royal lily grows to the height of three or four feet; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.29">Mt 6:29</reference> alludes to the beauty of its flowers.<div eID="gen22806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">roots as Lebanon--</hi>that is, as the trees of Lebanon (especially the cedars), which cast down their roots as deeply as is their height upwards; so that they are immovable [Jerome], (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.34">Is 10:34</reference>). Spiritual growth consists most in the growth of the root which is out of sight. <div eID="gen22807" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6c6200ef9f2ebd7ee6642c5c441acdccb39daec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12431"/><div sID="gen22808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12431"/><hi type="bold">6. branches--</hi>shoots, or suckers.<div eID="gen22808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beauty ... as the olive--</hi>which never loses its verdure. One plant is not enough to express the graces of God's elect people. The lily depicts its lovely growth; but as it wants duration and firmness, the deeply rooted cedars of Lebanon are added; these, however, are fruitless, therefore the fruitful, peace-bearing, fragrant, ever green olive is added.<div eID="gen22809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smell as Lebanon--</hi>which exhaled from it the fragrance of odoriferous trees and flowers. So Israel's name shall be in good savor with all (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.27">Ge 27:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.4.11">So 4:11</reference>). <div eID="gen22810" type="x-p"/>
entries.41e54d8c2ce339aa8c89f35e00b922a496ed4596: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12432"/><div sID="gen22811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12432"/>7. They that used to dwell under Israel's shadow (but who shall have been forced to leave it), shall return, that is, be restored (<reference osisRef="Ezek.35.9">Eze 35:9</reference>). Others take "His shadow" to mean Jehovah's (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.17.8">Psa 17:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.1">91:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Is 4:6</reference>), which <reference osisRef="Hos.14.1">Ho 14:1</reference>, 2 ("return unto the Lord," &c.) favor. But the "his" in <reference osisRef="Hos.14.6">Ho 14:6</reference> refers to Israel, and therefore must refer to the same here.<div eID="gen22811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">revive as ... corn--</hi>As the corn long buried in the earth springs up, with an abundant produce, so shall they revive from their calamities, with a great increase of offspring (compare <reference osisRef="John.12.24">Joh 12:24</reference>).<div eID="gen22812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scent thereof--</hi>that is, Israel's fame. Compare <reference osisRef="Hos.14.6">Ho 14:6</reference>, "His smell as Lebanon"; <reference osisRef="Song.1.3">So 1:3</reference>: "Thy name is as ointment poured forth." The Septuagint favors the Margin, "memorial."<div eID="gen22813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the wine of Lebanon--</hi>which was most celebrated for its aroma, flavor, and medicinal restorative properties. <div eID="gen22814" type="x-p"/>
entries.75a1b4240e48512032d1644574be5470505068a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12433"/><div sID="gen22815" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12433"/><hi type="bold">8. Ephraim shall say--</hi>being brought to penitence by God's goodness, and confessing and abhorring his past madness.<div eID="gen22815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I have heard ... and observed him--</hi>I Jehovah have answered and regarded him with favor; the opposite of God's "hiding His face from" one (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.17">De 31:17</reference>). It is the experience of God's favor, in contrast to God's wrath heretofore, that leads Ephraim to abhor his past idolatry. Jehovah heard and answered: whereas the idols, as Ephraim now sees, could not hear, much less answer.<div eID="gen22816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22817" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am ... a green fir--</hi>or cypress; ever green, winter and summer alike; the leaves not falling off in winter.<div eID="gen22817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">From me is thy fruit found--</hi>"From Me," as the root. Thou needest go no farther than Me for the supply of all thy wants; not merely the protection implied by the shadow of the cypress, but that which the cypress has not, namely, fruit, all spiritual and temporal blessings. It may be also implied, that whatever spiritual graces Ephraim seeks for or may have, are not of themselves, but of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.3">Psa 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.4">Joh 15:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.8">5, 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jas 1:17</reference>). God's promises to us are more our security for mortifying sin than our promises to God (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.9">Is 27:9</reference>). <div eID="gen22818" type="x-p"/>
entries.7b425877a95a56fe3cb84fc52325e2b125695c52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12434"/><div sID="gen22819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12434"/>9. Epilogue, summing up the whole previous teaching. Here alone Hosea uses the term "righteous," so rare were such characters in his day. There is enough of saving truth clear in God's Word to guide those humbly seeking salvation, and enough of difficulties to confound those who curiously seek them out, rather than practically seek salvation.<div eID="gen22819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fall--</hi>stumble and are offended at difficulties opposed to their prejudices and lusts, or above their self-wise understanding (compare <reference osisRef="Prov.10.29">Pr 10:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.2.7">Mi 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.19">Mt 11:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.34">Lu 2:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.7.17">Joh 7:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.7">1Pe 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.8">8</reference>). To him who sincerely seeks the agenda, God will make plain the credenda. Christ is the foundation-stone to some: a stone of stumbling and rock of offense to others. The same sun softens wax and hardens clay. But their fall is the most fatal who fall in the ways of God, split on the Rock of ages, and suck poison out of the Balm of Gilead. <chapter eID="Hos.14"/><div eID="gen22820" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen22269" osisID="Hos" type="book"/>

entries.4c81d41d46fa634a57de6bb9c70105bc76d31dc5: <div eID="gen33964" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33965" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33966" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33966" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33965" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33967" type="x-p"/> By the terrible denunciation of vengeance which concludes the preceding chapter, the prophet is led to exhort Israel to repentance, furnishing them with a beautiful form of prayer, very suitable to the occasion, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.1-Hos.14.3">Hos 14:1-3</reference>. Upon which God, ever ready to pardon the penitent, is introduced making large promises of blessings, in allusion to those copious dews which refresh the green herbs, and which frequently denote, not only temporal salvation, but also the rich and refreshing comforts of the Gospel, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.4-Hos.14.7">Hos 14:4-7</reference>. Their reformation from idolatry is foretold, and their consequent prosperity, under the emblem of a green flourishing fir tree, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.8">Hos 14:8</reference>; but these promises are confined to those who may bring forth the fruits of righteousness, and the wicked are declared to have no share in them, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.9">Hos 14:9</reference>. <div eID="gen33967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33968" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33969" type="x-p"/> O Israel, return unto the Lord - These words may be considered as addressed to the people now in captivity; suffering much, but having still much more to suffer if they did not repent. But it seems all these evils might yet be prevented, though so positively predicted, if the people would repent and return; and the very exhortation to this repentance shows that they still had power to repent, and that God was ready to save them and avert all these evils. All this is easily accounted for on the doctrine of the contingency of events, i.e., the poising a multitude of events on the possibility of being and not being, and leaving the will of man to turn the scale; and that God will not foreknow a thing as absolutely certain, which his will has determined to make contingent. A doctrine against which some solemn men have blasphemed, and philosophic infidels declaimed; but without which fate and dire necessity must be the universal governors, prayer be a useless meddling, and Providence nothing but the ineluctable adamantine chain of unchangeable events; all virtue is vice, and vice virtue, or there is no distinction between them, each being eternally determined and unalterably fixed by a sovereign and uncontrollable will and unvarying necessity, from the operation of which no soul of man can escape, and no occurrence in the universe be otherwise than it is. From such blasphemy, and from the monthly publications which avouch it, good Lord, deliver us!
entries.beef2c361aaf9fb474016c8041134920387a2ee5: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen33969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33970" type="x-p"/> Take with you words - And you may be assured that you pray aright, when you use the words which God himself has put in your mouths. On this very ground there is a potency in the Lord's Prayer, when offered up believingly, beyond what can be found in any human composition. And it may be presumed that it was this consideration that induced our reformers to introduce it so frequently in the public liturgy. <div eID="gen33970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33971" type="x-p"/> See the order of God's directions here: - <div eID="gen33971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33972" type="x-p"/> 1. Hearing these merciful invitations, believe them to be true. <div eID="gen33972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33973" type="x-p"/> 2. Cast aside your idols; and return to God as your Maker, King, and Savior. <div eID="gen33973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33974" type="x-p"/> 3. Take with you the words by which you have been encouraged, and plead them before God. <div eID="gen33974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33975" type="x-p"/> 4. Remember your iniquity, deeply deplore it, and beg of God to take it all away. <div eID="gen33975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33976" type="x-p"/> 5. Let faith be in exercise to receive what God waits to impart. "Receive us graciously;" וקח טוב vekach tob, receive, or let us receive good; when thou has emptied us of evil, fill us with goodness. <div eID="gen33976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33977" type="x-p"/> 6. Be then determined, through grace, to live to his glory, "so shall we render thee the calves" (פרים parim, for which the versions in general read פרי peri, fruits, omitting the ם mem) "of our lips;" the sacrifices of praise, thanksgiving, gratitude, and the hearty obedience which our lips have often promised. <div eID="gen33977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33978" type="x-p"/> 7. Having thus determined, specify your resolutions to depend on God alone for all that can make you wise, useful, holy, and happy. The resolutions are: - <div eID="gen33978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33979" type="x-p"/> 1. Asshur shall not save us - We will neither trust in, nor fear, this rich and powerful king. We will not look either to riches or power for true rest and peace of mind. <div eID="gen33979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33980" type="x-p"/> 2. We will not ride upon horses - We shall no more fix our hopes on the proud Egyptian cavalry, to deliver us out of the hands of enemies to whom thy Divine justice has delivered us. We will expect no rest nor happiness in the elegances of life, and gratification of our senses. <div eID="gen33980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33981" type="x-p"/> 3. Neither will we say any more to the work of our hands, Ye are our gods - We will not trust in any thing without us; nor even in any good thing we are able to do through thy grace; knowing we have nothing but what we have received. We will trust in thy infinite mercy for our final salvation. <div eID="gen33981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33982" type="x-p"/> 4. And we will do all this from the conviction, that in thee the fatherless findeth mercy; for we are all alike helpless, desolate, perishing orphans, till translated into thy family.
entries.779eb27e8f8bb5ba2e933bd4146f8d53f74e33e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33983" type="x-p"/> I will heal their backsliding - Here is the answer of God to these prayers and resolutions. See its parts: - <div eID="gen33983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33984" type="x-p"/> 1. Ye have backslidden and fallen, and are grievously and mortally wounded by that fall; but I, who am the Author of life, and who redeem from death, will heal all these wounds and spiritual diseases. <div eID="gen33984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33985" type="x-p"/> 2. I will love them freely - נדבה nedabah, after a liberal, princely manner. I will love them so as to do them incessant good. It shall not be a love of affection merely, but shall be a beneficial love. A love that not only feels delight in itself, but fills them with delight who are its objects, by making them unutterably and supremely happy. <div eID="gen33985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33986" type="x-p"/> 3. For mine anger is turned away from him - Because he has turned back to me. Thus God and man become friends.
entries.346848922cd9e790e498a7ef129df84d4af49e8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33987" type="x-p"/> I will be as the dew unto Israel - On these metaphors I gladly avail myself of the elegant and just observations of Bp. Lowth. "These verses (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.5-Hos.14.7">Hos 14:5-7</reference>) contain gracious promises of God's favor and blessings upon Israel's conversion. In the fifth verse, it is described by that refreshment which copious dews give to the grass in summer. If we consider the nature of the climate, and the necessity of dews in so hot a country, not only to refresh, but likewise to preserve life; if we consider also the beauty of the oriental lilies, the fragrance of the cedars which grow upon Lebanon, the beauteous appearance which the spreading olive trees afforded, the exhilarating coolness caused by the shade of such trees, and the aromatic smell exhaled by the cedars; we shall then partly understand the force of the metaphors here employed by the prophet; but their full energy no one can conceive, till he feels both the want, and enjoys the advantage, of the particulars referred to in that climate where the prophet wrote." - Lowth's twelfth and nineteenth prelection; and Dodd on the place. <div eID="gen33987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33988" type="x-p"/> What a glorious prophecy! What a wonderful prophet! How sublime, how energetic, how just! The great master prophet, Isaiah, alone could have done this better. And these promises are not for Israel merely after the flesh; they are for all the people of God. We have a lot and portion in the matter; God also places his love upon us. Here the reader must feel some such sentiment as the shepherd in Virgil, when enraptured with the elegy which his associate had composed on their departed friend. The phraseology and metaphors are strikingly similar; and therefore I shall produce it. <div eID="gen33988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33989" type="x-p"/> Tale tuum carmen nobis, divine poeta, <div eID="gen33989" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33990" type="x-p"/> Quale sopor fesses in gramine, quale per aestum <div eID="gen33990" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33991" type="x-p"/> Dulcis aquae saliente sitim restinguere rivo. <div eID="gen33991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33992" type="x-p"/> Nec calamis solum aequiparas, sed voce magistrum. <div eID="gen33992" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33993" type="x-p"/> Fortunate puer! tu nunc eris alter ab illo. <div eID="gen33993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33994" type="x-p"/> Nos tamen haec quocunque modo tibi nostra vicissim <div eID="gen33994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33995" type="x-p"/> Dicemus, Daphninque tuum tollemus ad astra: <div eID="gen33995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33996" type="x-p"/> Daphnin ad astra feremus: amavit nos quoque Daphnis. <div eID="gen33996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33997" type="x-p"/> Virgil. Ecl. v., ver. 45. "O heavenly poet, such thy verse appears, <div eID="gen33997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33998" type="x-p"/> So sweet, so charming to my ravish'd ears, <div eID="gen33998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33999" type="x-p"/> As to the weary swain with cares oppress'd, <div eID="gen33999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34000" type="x-p"/> Beneath the sylvan shade, refreshing rest; <div eID="gen34000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34001" type="x-p"/> As to the feverish traveler, when first <div eID="gen34001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34002" type="x-p"/> He finds a crystal stream to quench his thirst. <div eID="gen34002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34003" type="x-p"/> In singing, as in piping, you excel; <div eID="gen34003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34004" type="x-p"/> And scarce your master could perform so well. <div eID="gen34004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34005" type="x-p"/> O fortunate young man! at least your lays <div eID="gen34005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34006" type="x-p"/> Are next to his, and claim the second praise. <div eID="gen34006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34007" type="x-p"/> Such as they are, my rural songs I join <div eID="gen34007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34008" type="x-p"/> To raise your Daphnis to the powers divine; <div eID="gen34008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34009" type="x-p"/> For Daphnis was my friend, as well as thine."
entries.8d078bb8876cc1314d3b96538be64253cd47e847: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen34009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34010" type="x-p"/> They that dwell under his shadow shall return - The Targum is curious: "They shall be gathered together from the midst of their captivity; they shall dwell under the shadow of his Christ, and the dead shall revive." <div eID="gen34010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34011" type="x-p"/> They shall revive as the corn - The justness and beauty of this metaphor is not generally perceived. After the corn has been a short time above the earth, in a single spike, the blades begin to separate, and the stalk to spring out of the center. The side leaves turn back to make way for the protruding stalk; and fall bending down to the earth, assuming a withered appearance, though still attached to the plant. To look at the corn in this state, no one, unacquainted with the circumstance, could entertain any sanguine hope of a copious harvest. In a short time other leaves spring out; the former freshen, and begin to stand erect; and the whole seems to revive from a vegetative death. This is the circumstance to which the prophet refers "they shall revive as the corn." Of this a prudent and profitable use may be made. <div eID="gen34011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34012" type="x-p"/> 1. When a soul is first "drawn by the cords of love," <reference osisRef="Hos.11.4">Hos 11:4</reference>, every thing seems to it promising, comfortable, and delightful, like the corn in its first state. <div eID="gen34012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34013" type="x-p"/> 2. But when the Spirit of judgment brings to the light of conscience the hidden things of iniquity, and repentance is deepened into contrition, the broken and the contrite heart groans, and thinks that all is lost; deep distress takes place, and discouragement succeeds discouragement. This answers to the corn in its second state. <div eID="gen34013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34014" type="x-p"/> 3. By and by the pardon comes, and God's love is shed abroad in the heart by the Holy Ghost; every hope is revived and realized, the full corn in the ear becomes manifest; and this answers to the corn in its third state. "They shall revive as the corn." Glory be to God for his unspeakable gift!
entries.54569b6b027f7e2e1a2b27ab79c7ddde37125cb9: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen34014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34015" type="x-p"/> What have I to do any more with idols? - The conversion of Ephraim is now as complete as if was sincere. God hears and observes this. <div eID="gen34015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34016" type="x-p"/> I am like a green fir tree - Perhaps these words should be joined to the preceding, as Newcome has done, and be a part of God's speech to Ephraim. "I have heard him; and I have seen him as a flourishing fir tree." He is become strong and vigorous; and from his present appearance of healthiness, his future increase and prosperity may be safely anticipated. <div eID="gen34016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34017" type="x-p"/> From me is thy fruit found - All thy goodness springs from the principle of grace which I have planted in thy soul; for as the earth cannot bring forth fruit without the blessing of God, sending the dews and rains, with the genial rays of the sun, so neither can the soul of man, even of the most pious, bear fruit, without a continual influence from the Most High. Without the former, neither grass could grow for cattle, nor corn for the service of man; without the latter, no seeds of righteousness could take root, no stalk of promise could grow, no fruit of grace could be produced. And the unclean spirit, which was cast out, would soon return; and, finding his former house empty, swept, and garnished, would re-enter with seven demons of greater power and worse influence; and the latter end of that man would be worse than the first. Reader, ever consider that all thy good must be derived from God; and all that good must be preserved in thee by his continued influence of light, love, and power upon thy soul.
entries.795354a18fc6d287f78b681cfb9d845700b05019: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34018" type="x-p"/> Who is wise, and he shall understand these things? - What things? Those which relate to the backslidings, iniquity, and punishment of Israel; and to the mercy and kindness of God in their promised restoration. The things which belong to the work of sin in the heart; the things which belong to the work of grace in the soul; and particularly the things mentioned in this wonderful chapter. <div eID="gen34018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34019" type="x-p"/> Prudent, and he shall know them? - He who endeavors to understand them, who lays his heart to them, such a person shall understand them. <div eID="gen34019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34020" type="x-p"/> For the ways of the Lord are right - This is the conclusion which the prophet makes from the whole. All God's conduct, both in the dispensation of justice and mercy, is right: all as it should be, all as it must be; because he is too wise to err, too good to be unkind. <div eID="gen34020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34021" type="x-p"/> The just shall walk, in them - This is a truth which he will always acknowledge; and illustrate it by a righteous and godly life. <div eID="gen34021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34022" type="x-p"/> But the transgressors shall fall therein - Howsoever good they might have been before, if they do not consider the necessity of depending upon God; of receiving all their light, life, power, and love from him; ever evidencing that faith which worketh by love; maintaining an obedient conduct, and having respect to all God's precepts; they shall fall, even in the "way of righteousness." When still using the Divine ordinances, and associating with God's people, they shall perish from the way; and be like Ephraim, who once "spoke trembling," and "was exalted in Israel," who was "God's beloved son," and "called out of Egypt;" yet, by "offending in Baal," giving way to "the idols of his heart," fell from God, fell into the hands of his enemies, and became a wretched thrall in a heathen land. "Whoso is wise, let him understand these things! <div eID="gen34022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34023" type="x-p"/> Whoso is prudent, let him know them!" - <div eID="gen34023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34024" type="x-p"/> He who is well instructed will make a proper application of what he has here read; will tremble at the threatenings, and embrace the promises, of his God. <div eID="gen34024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34025" type="x-p"/> The Targum is worthy the most serious attention. "The ways of the Lord are right, and the just who walk in them shall live for ever; but the ungodly, because they have not walked in them, shall be delivered into hell." <div eID="gen34025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34026" type="x-p"/> How instructive, how convincing, how awakening, and yet how consolatory, are the words of this prophecy! Reader, lay them to heart. A godly mind cannot consider them in vain; such shall know them, and know that the ways of the Lord are right.  <chapter eID="Hos.14"/> <div eID="gen34026" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen33477" osisID="Hos" type="book"/>

entries.9e710684a73979bcb0d2a9ba4578ff96af8839c9: Hos 14:1-3 <div eID="gen16274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16275" type="x-p"/> After the prophet has set before the sinful nation in various ways its own guilt, and the punishment that awaits it, viz., the destruction of the kingdom, he concludes his addresses with a call to thorough conversion to the Lord, and the promise that the Lord will bestow His grace once more upon those who turn to Him, and will bless them abundantly (Hos 14:1-8). Hos 14:1. (Heb. Bib. v. 2). <hi type="italic">“Return, O Israel, to Jehovah thy God; for thou hast stumbled through thy guilt.</hi> Hos 14:2. <hi type="italic">Take with you words, and turn to Jehovah; say ye to Him, Forgive all guilt, and accept what is good, that we may offer our lips as bullocks.</hi> Hos 14:3. <hi type="italic">Asshur will not help us: we will not ride upon horses, nor say 'Our God' any more to the manufacture of our own hands; for with Thee the orphan findeth compassion.” </hi> There is no salvation for fallen man without return to God. It is therefore with a call to return to the Lord their God, that the prophet opens the announcement of the salvation with which the Lord will bless His people, whom He has brought to reflection by means of the judgment (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.30">Deu 4:30</reference>; Deu 30:1.). שׁוּב עד יי, to return, to be converted to the Lord, denotes complete conversion; שׁוּב אל is, strictly speaking, simply to turn towards God, to direct heart and mind towards Him. By <hi type="italic">kâshaltâ</hi> sin is represented as a false step, which still leaves it possible to return; so that in a call to conversion it is very appropriately chosen. But if the conversion is to be of the right kind, it must begin with a prayer for the forgiveness of sin, and attest itself by the renunciation of earthly help and simple trust in the mercy of God. Israel is to draw near to God in this state of mind. “Take with you words,” i.e., do not appear before the Lord empty (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.15">Exo 23:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.20">Exo 34:20</reference>); but for this ye do not require outward sacrifices, but simply words, sc. those of confession of your guilt, as the Chaldee has correctly explained it. The correctness of this explanation is evident from the confession of sin which follows, with which they are to come before God. In כּל־תּשּׂא עון, the position of <hi type="italic">col</hi> at the head of the sentence may be accounted for from the emphasis that rests upon it, and the separation of <hi type="italic">‛âvōn</hi>, from the fact that <hi type="italic">col</hi> was beginning to acquire more of the force of an adjective, like our <hi type="italic">all</hi> (thus <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.9">2Sa 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.3">Job 27:3</reference> : cf. Ewald, §289, <hi type="italic">a</hi>; Ges. §114, 3, Anm. 1). <hi type="italic">Qach tōbh</hi> means neither “accept goodness,” i.e., let goodness be shown thee (Hitzig), nor “take it as good,” sc. that we pray (Grotius, Ros.); but in the closest connection with what proceeds: Accept the only good thing that we are able to bring, viz., the sacrifices of our lips. Jerome has given the correct interpretation, viz.: “For unless Thou hadst borne away our evil things, we could not possibly have the good thing which we offer Thee;” according to that which is written elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.27">Psa 37:27</reference>), “Turn from evil, and do good.” שׂפתינוּ ... וּנשׁלּמה, literally, “we will repay (pay) as young oxen our lips,” i.e., present the prayers of our lips as thank-offerings. The expression is to be explained from the fact that <hi type="italic">shillēm</hi>, to wipe off what is owing, to pay, is a technical term, applied to the sacrifice offered in fulfilment of a vow (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.22">Deu 23:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.26">Psa 22:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.14">Psa 50:14</reference>, etc.), and that <hi type="italic">pârı̄m</hi>, young oxen, were the best animals for thank-offerings (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.5">Exo 24:5</reference>). As such thank-offerings, i.e., in the place of the best animal sacrifices, they would offer their lips, i.e., their prayers, to God (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.17-Ps.51.19">Psa 51:17-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.31-Ps.69.32">Psa 69:31-32</reference>). In the Sept. rendering, ἀποδώσομεν καρπὸν χείλεων, to which there is an allusion in <reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb 13:15</reference>, פּרים has been confounded with פּרי, as Jerome has already observed. but turning to God requires renunciation of the world, of its power, and of all idolatry. Rebellious Israel placed its reliance upon Assyria and Egypt (Hos 5:13; Hos 7:11; Hos 8:9). It will do this no longer. The riding upon horses refers partly to the military force of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">Isa 31:1</reference>), and partly to their own (Hos 1:7; <reference osisRef="Isa.2.7">Isa 2:7</reference>). For the expression, “neither will we say to the work of our hands,” compare <reference osisRef="Isa.42.17">Isa 42:17</reference>; Isa 44:17. אשׁר בּך, not “Thou with whom,” but “for with Thee” (<hi type="italic">'ăsher</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Deut.3.24">Deu 3:24</reference>). The thought, “with Thee the orphan findeth compassion,” as God promises in His word (<reference osisRef="Exod.22.22">Exo 22:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.10.18">Deu 10:18</reference>), serves not only as a reason for the resolution no longer to call the manufacture of their own hands God, but generally for the whole of the penitential prayer, which they are encouraged to offer by the compassionate nature of God. In response to such a penitential prayer, the Lord will heal all His people’s wounds, and bestow upon them once more the fulness of the blessings of His grace. The prophet announces this in <reference osisRef="Isa.44.4-Isa.44.8">Isa 44:4-8</reference> as the answer from the Lord.
entries.94f46106fc5713b068af988b49dbeb285b8ec83f: Hos 14:4-8 <hi type="italic">“I will heal their apostasy, will love them freely: for my wrath has turned away from it. </hi> Hos 14:5. <hi type="italic">I will be like dew for Israel: it shall blossom like the lily, and strike its roots like Lebanon.</hi> Hos 14:6. <hi type="italic">Its shoots shall go forth, and its splendour shall become like the olive-tree, and its smell like Lebanon. </hi> Hos 14:7. <hi type="italic">They that dwell in its shadow shall give life to corn again; and shall blossom like the vine: whose glory is like the wine of Lebanon.</hi> Hos 14:8. <hi type="italic">Ephraim: What have I further with the idols? I hear, and look upon him: I, like a bursting cypress, in me is thy fruit found.” </hi> The Lord promises first of all to heal their apostasy, i.e., all the injuries which have been inflicted by their apostasy from Him, and to love them with perfect spontaneity (<hi type="italic">nedâbhâh</hi> an adverbial accusative, <hi type="italic">promta animi voluntate</hi>), since His anger, which was kindled on account of its idolatry, had now turned away from it (<hi type="italic">mimmennū</hi>, i.e., from Israel). The reading <hi type="italic">mimmennı̄</hi> (from me), which the Babylonian Codices have after the Masora, appears to have originated in a misunderstanding of Jer 2:35. This love of the Lord will manifest itself in abundant blessing. Jehovah will be to Israel a refreshing, enlivening dew (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">Isa 26:19</reference>), through which it will blossom splendidly, strike deep roots, and spread its shoots far and wide. “Like the lily:” the fragrant white lily, which is very common in Palestine, and grows without cultivation, and “which is unsurpassed in its fecundity, often producing fifty bulbs from a single root” (Pliny <hi type="italic">h. n.</hi> xxi. 5). “Strike roots like Lebanon,” i.e., not merely the deeply rooted forest of Lebanon, but the mountain itself, as one of the “foundations of the earth” (Mic 6:2). The deeper the roots, the more the branches spread and cover themselves with splendid green foliage, like the evergreen and fruitful olive-tree (<reference osisRef="Jer.11.16">Jer 11:16</reference>; Ps. 52:10). The smell is like Lebanon, which is rendered fragrant by its cedars and spices (Sol 4:11).
